Can You Do London with a Toddler? Yes — Here’s How

  • By Tanvi Chheda
  • August 23, 2026
  • 6 Min Read
London England UK Europe Traveling with Babies and Toddlers
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:15
Instaread

Historic, iconic and royal, London brings to mind sites such as Tower Bridge, Westminster Abbey and Buckingham Palace, not to mention cultural spots like Shakespeare’s Globe, the National Gallery and the Tate Modern. And it’s full of charming neighborhoods with flower shops, pint-size cafes and trendy bars.

Is it possible to soak up some of this atmosphere in with a toddler in tow? Yes — a resounding yes. It may require adjusting expectations, but seeing London with a toddler will rouse a sense of wonder in both parent and child.

Children, especially toddlers, are inherently curious, not to mention intrepid! They’ll turn a corner and lead you down a new path, walk up to strangers, stroll through the Tube car with a grin on the their face. True, it takes patience and flexibility to navigate a vast city with a little one. But to see your toddler’s eyes fill with awe as a double-decker bus whizzes by or as they approach the Diana Princess of Wales Memorial Playground in Kensington Gardens is also a memory to cherish.

Below are some tips and suggestions for seeing London from a young child’s eyes.

Essential Tips for Visiting London with Toddlers in Tow

Parks and Gardens

You’re likely thinking you didn’t come all this way simply to visit a park or garden, but the British, in fact, have a national obsession with gardens themselves. Gardens have long been places for respite, places to express creativity and, of course, places to host garden parties. And so, Kew Gardens, officially the Royal Botanic Gardens, is a great place to take toddlers; it has a dedicated Children’s Garden for ages 2 to 12. Don’t miss Hyde Park either: A green oasis in a teeming city, much like New York’s Central Park, the 350-acre expanse was created by Henry VIII in 1536. It’s an ideal reset button after a morning of sightseeing — let toddlers run around, watch the ducks and geese, explore the playgrounds and take a break from London’s busy streets.

In Kensington Gardens, the Diana Princess of Wales Memorial Playground recently reopened after a £3 million renovation. This Peter Pan-inspired space has a new wooden galleon, treehouse, water play area and dedicated area for under-3s. It’s free to enter and particularly well suited to toddlers. You could also combine park playtime with a zoo visit: Regents Park houses the famed London Zoo, while the more off-path Battersea Park is home to the Battersea Children’s Zoo (perfect for the stroller set).

Historic Sites, Museums and Toy Stores

Though it is challenging to see some of the top historic sites with a toddler, there are alternate ways to experience them. Rather than trying to take a serious guided tour of the interior of Buckingham Palace, head to the Royal Mews, which serves as the King’s garage. It’s home to his collection of cars and carriages, as well as horse stables. Transport vehicles and animals are a guaranteed hit with any toddler!

A few other sites that are easier for younger ones include the stroller-friendly Millennium Bridge and a ride on the London Eye, or ambling around Trafalgar Square. And while it might feel like a bit of a tourist trap, a hop-on/hop-off double-decker bus may well be the highlight of a 3-year-old’s day and a fantastic way to get a quick overview of the city.

Young V&A in Bethnal Green, an offshoot of the flagship V&A Museum, is one of the city’s absolute best toddler museums. Its Play Gallery includes sensory spaces, dress-up, building areas and other hands-on activities for young children. While the Natural History Museum is well known, the neighboring Science Museum is more of a hidden gem, and it features multisensory play zones designed specifically for littles. Admission to both Young V&A and the Science Museum is free, making it easier to cut your losses if your toddler gets fussy.

How it Works

Another favorite of local parents, the hands-on London Transport Museum is perfect for curious toddlers. Showcasing 200 years of London’s transport history with colorful maps and displays, the museum houses double-decker buses, old trams, Tube cars and trains, all just waiting for toddlers to climb aboard. The museum’s gift shop is also top-notch, with plenty of Tube and Mind the Gap paraphernalia.

For more toys and gifts, consider Hamleys, a seven-story toy emporium dating back to 1760 in the heart of London’s shopping district along Regent Street. You’ll find it hard to escape without a purchase in hand, but many of the unique and special toys are set out for toddlers to try and play with. Plus, the top floor features the royal family made out of Legos!

A Children’s Tea

Afternoon tea is the quintessential British experience as well as a chance to dress up and feel special. At the Ampersand Hotel in South Kensington, the science-themed tea lets kids make fizzy drinks in beakers and excavate chocolate fossils between courses. For a bigger occasion, Aqua Shard‘s Peter Pan tea is served 31 floors up, with treats on a stand shaped like Captain Hook’s pirate ship and scones hidden in a treasure chest.

If your toddler tends to get antsy sitting through meals, Brigit’s Bakery serves afternoon tea aboard a vintage Routemaster bus, looping past Big Ben and Tower Bridge while an onboard entertainer keeps the youngest guests occupied. The Peppa Pig, Paw Patrol and Paddington tours work great for ages 2 and up … you get sightseeing and tea in one, and you won’t feel pressure to make your kids sit still.

Practical Points

  • From Heathrow, the Heathrow Express is the fastest option to Paddington Station, taking about 15 minutes, while the Tube’s Elizabeth line offers direct service to several central London stations and may be more convenient depending on where you’re staying. Families with lots of luggage might find that a taxi or private transfer into town is easiest, despite the typically heavy Heathrow traffic.
  • Be strategic about where you stay. Being within walking distance or a short Tube ride of the attractions and areas you plan to visit makes a world of difference with a toddler; you don’t want to spend too much time getting where you need to go. Both Mayfair and Kensington are central areas with many hotel and stay options across price points.
  • The Tube can be challenging with a stroller, but don’t rule it out. Many stations aren’t step-free, so check your route before setting out and consider a lightweight, foldable stroller. Buses are sometimes easier with young children, and they offer a bonus: Kids under 11 travel free.
  • While London restaurants aren’t known for catering to kids as those in, say, Italy, it has plenty of sophisticated venues that welcome families. You’ll want to check age policies and make reservations in advance. That said, earlier dinner times and relaxed restaurants are usually the easiest fit with toddlers. There’s a bottomless pool of informal eats that are plenty delicious, and the Borough Market food hall offers dozens of stalls and purveyors (go at off-peak times to avoid the worst of the crowds).
